questions.explanation: The equation gives $S = CA^Z$, so $\frac{S_2}{S_1} = 100^{0.2} = 10^{0.4} \approx 2.51$. This gives about 502 species. Species richness rises much more slowly than area, so a proportional (linear) increase is the trap.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: According to Robert May, approximately how many species exist on earth? This is described as a conservative and scientifically sound estimate.
questions.explanation: Robert May estimated global species diversity at about 7 million. The figure of 1.5 million is the number of species described so far, and 20–50 million are the extreme estimates.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Strict protection of biodiversity hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.
Reason (R): Although all hotspots together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area, they collectively harbour an extremely high number of species.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Hotspots pack a very large share of species into a small area. That is exactly why protecting them yields a large cut (about 30%) in extinctions, so R correctly explains A.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Mammals and birds that need large territories, and animals with migratory habits, are badly affected by habitat fragmentation.
Reason (R): In fragmentation, large habitats are broken up into small fragments by various human activities.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: When a large habitat is broken into small patches, no single patch can meet the needs of animals requiring large territories or migratory routes, so their populations decline. R therefore correctly explains A.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Arrange the following groups in decreasing order of the percentage of their species currently facing the threat of extinction worldwide:
(A) Birds
(B) Mammals
(C) Amphibians
(D) Gymnosperms
questions.explanation: The threatened proportions are amphibians 32%, gymnosperms 31%, mammals 23% and birds 12%. Amphibians and gymnosperms differ by only one per cent, so they are easy to swap.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following statements regarding estimation of global species diversity are correct?
I. Biologists estimate the total number of species by extrapolating the temperate-tropical species richness ratio of an exhaustively studied group of insects to other groups of plants and animals.
II. For many taxonomic groups, species inventories are more complete in tropical countries than in temperate countries.
III. Plants, a group that here includes algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, make up no more than 22 per cent of all recorded species.
IV. Robert May regarded the extreme estimates of 20 to 50 million species as the most scientifically sound.
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II reverses the fact: inventories are more complete in temperate countries, which is why the tropical shortfall has to be extrapolated. Statement IV is wrong because May's own estimate of about 7 million is the conservative one, and the 20 to 50 million figures are called extreme.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following recently extinct organisms is INCORRECTLY paired with the region it belonged to?
questions.explanation: The thylacine belonged to Australia, not Africa. The quagga is the African example of recent extinction, so this pairing is a likely source of confusion.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (region) with List-II (approximate number of bird species).
List-I:
A. Colombia
B. New York
C. Greenland
D. India
List-II:
I. 56
II. More than 1,200
III. 105
IV. Nearly 1,400
questions.explanation: Colombia has nearly 1,400 bird species, New York 105, Greenland 56 and India more than 1,200. A common trap is swapping Colombia and India, since both have high, similar counts.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Tropical environments promote niche specialisation, leading to greater species diversity.
Reason (R): Tropical environments are less seasonal and relatively more constant and predictable than temperate environments.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: NCERT's second hypothesis states that constant, predictable tropical conditions allow organisms to specialise for narrow niches. That specialisation raises species diversity. So R directly explains A.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: When species richness is plotted against area on ordinary (arithmetic) axes for taxa such as angiosperms, birds, bats and freshwater fishes, the curve obtained is a:
options: Straight line passing through the origin
questions.explanation: On ordinary axes the species–area relationship is a rectangular hyperbola. It becomes a straight line only when both axes are on a logarithmic scale.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: India's share of the global species diversity is about:
questions.explanation: India holds about 8.1% of the world's recorded species on only 2.4% of its land. This disproportionately high share makes India biologically rich.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The tropics, which harbour more species than temperate or polar areas, are defined by which latitudinal range?
questions.explanation: NCERT defines the tropics as the belt from $23.5^\circ$ N to $23.5^\circ$ S. With very few exceptions, this belt holds more species than higher latitudes. The $66.5^\circ$ value marks the polar circles, not the tropics.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (symbols in $\log S = \log C + Z \log A$) with List-II (their meaning).
List-I:
(a) S
(b) A
(c) Z
(d) C
List-II:
(i) Y-intercept
(ii) Regression coefficient
(iii) Species richness
(iv) Area
questions.explanation: S is species richness, A is area, Z is the slope (regression coefficient) and C is the Y-intercept. A common trap is to swap the slope and the intercept.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in Johannesburg in 2002, how many countries pledged to significantly reduce the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010?
questions.explanation: At Johannesburg, 190 countries committed to achieving a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss by 2010. The number 34 is the count of biodiversity hotspots, and 12 is the number of mega diversity countries.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Nearly 45,000 species of plants have been recorded from India. Approximately how many animal species have been recorded from the country?
questions.explanation: India has recorded about twice as many animal species as plant species, which is roughly 90,000. The figure of 3,00,000 is the estimate of animal species still undiscovered, not those already recorded.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of sacred grove region and state, as given in NCERT, is INCORRECT?
options: Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas – Madhya Pradesh
Western Ghat regions – Karnataka and Maharashtra
questions.explanation: The Khasi and Jaintia Hills are in Meghalaya, not Assam. There the sacred groves are the last refuges for many rare and threatened plants. The other three pairings match NCERT.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The term 'biodiversity' describes the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation. Who popularised this term?
questions.explanation: NCERT credits the sociobiologist Edward Wilson with popularising the term biodiversity. Ehrlich proposed the rivet popper hypothesis, May estimated global species numbers, and Humboldt studied species–area relationships.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (regions with sacred groves) with List-II (state in which they lie, as given in NCERT).
List-I:
A. Khasi and Jaintia Hills
B. Aravalli Hills
C. Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas
D. Western Ghat regions
List-II:
I. Rajasthan
II. Karnataka and Maharashtra
III. Meghalaya
IV. Madhya Pradesh
questions.explanation: The Khasi-Jaintia Hills are in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills in Rajasthan, the Sarguja-Chanda-Bastar areas in Madhya Pradesh (as per NCERT), and the Western Ghat sacred groves in Karnataka and Maharashtra.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which one of the following is an example of ex situ conservation?
questions.explanation: Wildlife safari parks, zoological parks and botanical gardens keep threatened organisms outside their natural habitat, so they are ex situ methods. National parks, sacred groves and biosphere reserves protect species in their natural habitat, which is in situ conservation.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: According to the IUCN (2004), roughly how many plant and animal species have been described so far?
questions.explanation: IUCN (2004) put the number of described plant and animal species at slightly more than 1.5 million. The larger figures are estimates of total species, not counts of described species.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Statement I: The approach summed up as 'we save the entire forest to save the tiger' is an example of ex situ conservation.
Statement II: Biodiversity hotspots are also regions of accelerated habitat loss.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: Protecting the whole ecosystem so that all its biodiversity is saved is in situ (on site) conservation, so Statement I is false. NCERT states that hotspots are also regions of accelerated habitat loss, so Statement II is true.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the rivet popper analogy, losing rivets from the wings of the airplane is a more serious threat to flight safety than losing a few rivets from the seats or windows.
Reason (R): The wing rivets represent key species that drive major ecosystem functions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Ehrlich stressed that which rivet is removed matters. Wing rivets symbolise key species driving major ecosystem functions, so their loss endangers the ecosystem more, and R directly explains A.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (parts of the rivet popper analogy) with List-II (what they represent):
List-I
A. Airplane
B. Rivets
C. A passenger popping a rivet
D. Flight safety
List-II
I. Species becoming extinct
II. Proper functioning of the ecosystem
III. Ecosystem
IV. Species
Choose the correct answer:
questions.explanation: The airplane is the ecosystem and the rivets are species. Popping a rivet means a species going extinct, and flight safety means proper ecosystem functioning.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Pollination by bees, birds and bats is cited under the broadly utilitarian argument for conserving biodiversity.
Reason (R): The broadly utilitarian argument holds that biodiversity plays a major role in the ecosystem services that nature provides.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Pollination is an ecosystem service, and the broadly utilitarian argument is defined by such services. So R correctly explains A.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the species–area relationship is INCORRECT?
options: When species richness and area are both plotted on a logarithmic scale, the relationship becomes a straight line
For analyses within a region, the slope Z depends strongly on the taxonomic group, so plants and birds give very different Z values
Analyses across very large areas such as entire continents give much steeper slopes, with Z of about 0.6 to 1.2
For frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, the slope is about 1.15
questions.explanation: Within a region, Z lies between 0.1 and 0.2 regardless of the taxonomic group or region, so the regression slopes are remarkably similar. Only continent-scale analyses give much steeper slopes.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
In the global species inventory, how many of the following groups are included in the 'plants' category that makes up no more than 22 per cent of recorded species?
Algae, Fungi, Bryophytes, Gymnosperms, Angiosperms, Insects, Molluscs
questions.explanation: NCERT counts algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms under plants, which makes five groups. Insects and molluscs are animals; the common trap is leaving out fungi.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the species–area equation $\log S = \log C + Z \log A$, the term $Z$ represents:
options: The slope of the line (regression coefficient)
questions.explanation: $Z$ is the slope of the log–log regression line. $S$ is species richness, $A$ is area and $C$ is the Y-intercept.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Statement I: In Tilman's experiments, increased species diversity contributed to higher productivity.
Statement II: Ecologists have given a definitive answer to whether the number of species in a community affects ecosystem functioning.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation: Tilman did show that higher diversity increased productivity. However, NCERT states that ecologists have not been able to give a definitive answer, and Tilman's results are only tentative.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The slopes of the species–area regression lines for plants in Britain, birds in California and molluscs in New York state are remarkably similar.
Reason (R): Within a region, the value of $Z$ depends strongly on the taxonomic group being studied.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Within regions, $Z$ stays around 0.1–0.2 regardless of the taxonomic group or the region. That is exactly why these very different groups show similar slopes, so R contradicts the observation.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The 'Sixth Extinction' now in progress differs from the five earlier mass extinctions in earth's history mainly because
options: it is affecting only plant species, whereas earlier ones affected animals
current extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times
it is caused by glaciations, whereas earlier ones were caused by volcanic activity
it is occurring at a rate 10 times slower than in pre-human times
questions.explanation: The key difference is the rate. Present extinctions are 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and human activities are responsible for this acceleration.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is regarded as having the greatest biodiversity on earth?
options: Temperate forests of the Midwest USA
The Amazonian rain forest of South America
questions.explanation: The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest is described as having the greatest biodiversity on earth. Western Ghats is a hotspot, but it is not the richest region overall.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match each cause of biodiversity loss in List-I with the example in List-II.
List-I
A. Habitat loss
B. Over-exploitation
C. Alien species invasion
D. Co-extinction
List-II
(i) Disappearance of a host fish's unique assemblage of parasites
(ii) Extinction of Steller's sea cow
(iii) Clearing of the Amazon forest for soya bean cultivation
(iv) Loss of more than 200 cichlid species in Lake Victoria
Choose the correct option:
questions.explanation: Amazon clearing is habitat loss. Steller's sea cow was hunted to extinction (over-exploitation). The cichlids were lost after the Nile perch was introduced (alien invasion). Parasites die out with their host (co-extinction).
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (scientist) with List-II (contribution) and choose the correct option.
List-I
A. Edward Wilson
B. Robert May
C. Paul Ehrlich
D. David Tilman
List-II
I. Rivet popper hypothesis
II. Popularised the term 'biodiversity'
III. Long-term outdoor plot experiments linking diversity with productivity
IV. Estimate of global species diversity at about 7 million
questions.explanation: Wilson, a sociobiologist, popularised the term biodiversity. May gave the conservative estimate of about 7 million species. Ehrlich proposed the rivet popper analogy, and Tilman ran the outdoor plot experiments.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following are examples of in situ conservation?
Biosphere reserves, seed banks, national parks, zoological parks, sacred groves, cryopreservation of gametes, wildlife sanctuaries, botanical gardens
questions.explanation: Biosphere reserves, national parks, sacred groves and wildlife sanctuaries protect species within their natural ecosystems, so they are in situ (4). Seed banks, zoos, cryopreservation and botanical gardens remove organisms or their gametes from the habitat, so they are ex situ.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: India is recognised as one of how many megadiversity countries of the world?
questions.explanation: India is one of the 12 megadiversity countries. The other numbers belong to different facts: 25 and 34 are the initial and current counts of biodiversity hotspots, and 14 is the number of biosphere reserves in India.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following statements about the species–area relationship are correct?
(a) On arithmetic axes, species richness increases linearly with area.
(b) Species richness keeps increasing with area without any limit.
(c) On a log–log scale, the relationship becomes a straight line.
(d) For very large areas such as entire continents, $Z$ ranges from 0.6 to 1.2.
(e) In the equation, C is the Y-intercept.
(f) The relationship has been shown for angiosperms, birds, bats and freshwater fishes.
questions.explanation: Statements (c), (d), (e) and (f) are correct, giving four. Statement (a) is wrong because the arithmetic curve is a rectangular hyperbola, and (b) is wrong because Humboldt found richness rises only up to a limit.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): For a plant species facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild in the near future and needing urgent measures, in situ conservation is the desirable approach.
Reason (R): In situ conservation protects the whole ecosystem, so biodiversity at all its levels is protected.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: R is true: saving the whole forest to save the tiger protects diversity at all levels. A is false, because NCERT says ex situ (off-site) conservation is the desirable approach for endangered or threatened organisms needing urgent rescue.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following are ex situ approaches to biodiversity conservation?
Sacred groves, seed banks, cryopreservation of gametes, wildlife safari parks, biosphere reserves, national parks, botanical gardens
questions.explanation: Four of the listed approaches are ex situ: seed banks, cryopreservation of gametes, wildlife safari parks and botanical gardens. Sacred groves, biosphere reserves and national parks protect organisms in their natural habitat, so they are in situ. Safari parks are a common trap, but NCERT lists them as ex situ.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Statement I: The relatively constant and predictable environments of the tropics promote niche specialisation, which leads to greater species diversity.
Statement II: The greater solar energy received by the tropics directly increases the rate of speciation, without any role of productivity.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation: Statement I matches the niche specialisation hypothesis. Statement II is incorrect because more solar energy raises productivity, and this only indirectly contributes to greater diversity, not directly.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (example) with List-II (cause of biodiversity loss):
List-I
A. Steller's sea cow
B. Parthenium in India
C. Parasites of an extinct host fish
D. Amazon forest cleared for soya beans
List-II
I. Co-extinction
II. Habitat loss
III. Over-exploitation
IV. Alien species invasion
questions.explanation: Steller's sea cow was hunted to extinction (over-exploitation), and Parthenium is an invasive alien weed. A host fish's unique parasites die out with it (co-extinction), and clearing the Amazon for soya is habitat loss.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis, what do the thousands of rivets holding the airplane together represent?
questions.explanation: In the analogy each rivet stands for a species, and the airplane stands for the ecosystem. A common trap is to equate rivets with individuals or with the ecosystem itself.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The Western Ghats have a greater diversity of amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats. This comparison illustrates diversity at which level?
questions.explanation: Comparing the number of amphibian species in two regions is a measure of species diversity. Genetic diversity refers to variation within one species.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: David Tilman's long-term experiments on species richness and ecosystem stability were carried out using:
questions.explanation: NCERT describes Tilman's work as long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots. Plots with differing numbers of species were compared over many years.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following benefits fall under the narrowly utilitarian argument for conserving biodiversity?
Tannins, flood control, resins, firewood, aesthetic pleasure of watching spring flowers, perfumes, pollination by bats
questions.explanation: Tannins, resins, firewood and perfumes are direct economic products, which makes four. Flood control and pollination are ecosystem services, and aesthetic pleasure is an intangible benefit, so all three are broadly utilitarian.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following statements about biodiversity loss are correct?
(a) The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species in the last 500 years.
(b) Current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times.
(c) About 23 per cent of all bird species in the world face the threat of extinction.
(d) Extinctions are random across taxa, with no group more vulnerable than another.
(e) About 32 per cent of all amphibian species face the threat of extinction.
questions.explanation: Statements (a), (b) and (e) are correct. About 12% of bird species are threatened; the 23% figure refers to mammals. Extinctions are not random, since amphibians appear more vulnerable.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The argument that every species deserves protection because it has an intrinsic value, even if it has no economic value to humans, is the:
questions.explanation: The ethical argument rests on the intrinsic value of every species and on our moral duty to pass on our biological legacy in good order. Both utilitarian arguments depend on some benefit to humans.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Some animal species that have become extinct in the wild still exist on earth.
Reason (R): Ex situ conservation keeps threatened animals outside their natural habitat, for example in zoological parks, where they receive protection and special care.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Many animals that are extinct in the wild survive only because they are maintained in zoological parks, which is an ex situ setting. R therefore directly explains why A is true.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Tropical latitudes generally harbour more species than temperate regions.
Reason (R): Tropical regions were subjected to frequent glaciations in the past, which repeatedly triggered new speciation.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The Assertion is true. The Reason is false because it was the temperate regions that faced frequent glaciations. The tropics stayed relatively undisturbed for millions of years, which gave them a long evolutionary time for species diversification.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the context of the latitudinal gradient of biodiversity, the tropics are defined as the region lying between which latitudes?
questions.explanation: The tropics extend from 23.5° N to 23.5° S of the equator, on both sides. A belt north of the equator alone is not the tropics, and 66.5° marks the polar circles.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The Amazon rain forest is estimated to produce what percentage of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere through photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: The Amazon is estimated to supply about 20 per cent of atmospheric oxygen, which is an ecosystem service. The figures 6 and 14 per cent describe how much of the earth's land surface rain forests cover now and once covered.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Read the two statements about recorded global biodiversity.
Statement I: The number of fungal species in the world exceeds the combined number of species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.
Statement II: Among animals, molluscs form the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of animal species.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation: NCERT states that fungal species outnumber fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals combined, so Statement I is correct. Statement II is incorrect because insects, not molluscs, are the most species-rich animal group, forming more than 70 per cent of animal species. In other words, roughly 7 of every 10 animals are insects.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate inference that can be drawn from Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis?
options: The extinction of even a single species always causes immediate collapse of the ecosystem
All species contribute equally to ecosystem functioning, so only the total number of species lost matters
A few extinctions may not visibly affect ecosystem functioning at first, but continued losses progressively weaken it, and losing key species is especially damaging
Since early species losses do not affect ecosystem functioning, biodiversity loss is harmless until a precisely calculable number of species is lost
questions.explanation: The analogy says early rivet loss may not affect flight safety, but the plane weakens as more rivets go, and wing rivets matter more. This rules out immediate collapse, equal contribution, and a 'harmless up to a calculable threshold' view.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): To estimate the total number of species on earth, biologists compare the temperate-tropical species richness of an exhaustively studied insect group and extrapolate this ratio to other groups.
Reason (R): For many taxonomic groups, species inventories are more complete in temperate than in tropical countries, while most undiscovered species are in the tropics.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Tropical inventories are incomplete and hold most undiscovered species. A ratio from a well-studied group is therefore needed to extrapolate totals, so R directly justifies the method described in A.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match the recently extinct animals in List-I with the regions where they lived in List-II.
List-I
(a) Dodo
(b) Quagga
(c) Thylacine
(d) Steller's sea cow
List-II
(i) Russia
(ii) Australia
(iii) Mauritius
(iv) Africa
questions.explanation: NCERT lists the dodo from Mauritius, the quagga from Africa, the thylacine from Australia and Steller's sea cow from Russia. A common slip is placing the dodo in Africa because Mauritius is an African island nation.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following statements regarding loss of biodiversity are correct?
(i) In the extinctions documented by the IUCN Red List (2004) for the last 500 years, invertebrates outnumber vertebrates.
(ii) Loss of biodiversity in a region lowers its resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought.
(iii) Loss of biodiversity reduces the variability of pest and disease cycles in an ecosystem.
(iv) Careful analysis of records shows that extinctions occur randomly across all taxa.
(v) The Bali, Javan and Caspian tigers are extinct subspecies of tiger.
questions.explanation: Statements (i), (ii) and (v) are correct, since the Red List records 359 invertebrate versus 338 vertebrate extinctions. Statement (iii) is wrong because biodiversity loss increases variability in processes such as pest and disease cycles. Statement (iv) is wrong because extinctions are non-random, and groups like amphibians are more vulnerable.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following are invasive weed species cited by NCERT as threats to native Indian species?
Parthenium, Lantana, Eichhornia, Clarias gariepinus, Nile perch
questions.explanation: Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana and Eichhornia (water hyacinth) are invasive weeds. Clarias gariepinus and Nile perch are invasive alien species, but they are fish, not weeds.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Large-scale loss of species is not a phenomenon unique to the period after humans appeared on Earth.
Reason (R): Current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: A is true because fossil records show five mass extinctions before humans existed. R is also true, but it describes how the present episode differs from those events, so it does not explain why mass extinctions are not unique to the human era.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following are among the hypotheses given in NCERT to explain the greater species richness of the tropics?
(a) Tropical latitudes remained relatively undisturbed by glaciations, giving a long evolutionary time for speciation
(b) Tropical environments are less seasonal and more predictable
(c) More solar energy in the tropics contributes to higher productivity
(d) Tropical regions have lower rates of habitat loss than temperate regions
(e) Frequent glaciations in the tropics created many isolated refuges that promoted speciation
questions.explanation: Only (a), (b) and (c) are the NCERT hypotheses, so the count is three. Statement (d) is false, since tropical rain forests are suffering the most dramatic habitat loss. Statement (e) is false because NCERT links glaciations to temperate regions, not to the tropics.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
How many of the following are hypotheses proposed to explain the greater species richness of the tropics?
(i) The tropics have had a long evolutionary time, undisturbed by frequent glaciations
(ii) Tropical environments are highly seasonal and unpredictable
(iii) Constant, predictable environments promote niche specialisation
(iv) More solar energy in the tropics contributes to higher productivity
(v) The tropics experienced more frequent glaciations, which stimulated speciation
questions.explanation: Statements (i), (iii) and (iv) are the three proposed hypotheses. Statement (ii) is wrong because tropical environments are less seasonal. Statement (v) is wrong because frequent glaciations affected temperate regions, not the tropics.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
Match List-I (example) with List-II (category of argument for conserving biodiversity):
List-I
A. Resins, dyes and lubricants obtained from plants
B. Pollination of crops by bumblebees and bats
C. Moral duty to pass on our biological legacy to future generations
D. Joy of waking up to a bulbul's song
List-II
I. Ethical
II. Narrowly utilitarian
III. Broadly utilitarian (intangible benefit)
IV. Broadly utilitarian (ecosystem service)
questions.explanation: Industrial products are direct economic benefits, so they are narrowly utilitarian. Pollination is an ecosystem service and aesthetic pleasure is an intangible benefit, both broadly utilitarian. Moral duty belongs to the ethical argument.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: During his explorations of South American jungles, which naturalist observed that, within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit?
questions.explanation: The German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt first described the species-area relationship. Wilson popularised the term biodiversity, May estimated global species numbers, and Tilman ran long-term plot experiments on diversity and stability.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Using NCERT's figures, a student wants to know roughly what share of all recorded species (plants, animals and fungi together) are insects. Animals are just over 70 per cent of recorded species, and insects are just over 70 per cent of animals. The closest estimate is:
questions.explanation: Insects make up just over 70 per cent of an animal share that is itself just over 70 per cent, and 0.7 × 0.7 ≈ 0.5, so roughly half of all recorded species are insects. The trap is answering 70 per cent, which is the insect share of animals only.
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation
